title: Conversational stream middleware sandbox and developer guide
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Engineers building conversational features with the Python SDK repeatedly re-implement the same small pieces when consuming streaming chat: sanitizing developer signals, wiring retry/backoff logic, de-duplicating partial deltas, and composing sideband sinks (telemetry, transcript capture, metrics). This leads to inconsistent behavior across apps and bloated example code.

Goal: Ship a small but composable middleware sandbox in the Python SDK that provides a minimal, well-documented API for common streaming concerns and a companion developer guide and example repository. The middleware should be usable both as a quick import for apps and as a test harness for deterministic replay of recorded streams.

Scope:
- Define a tiny middleware contract (async callables/hooks) that can adapt both generator-style and async-iterator style stream consumers.
- Provide 3 official middleware primitives: signal_sanitizer, idempotent_sink_wrapper, retry_bridge.
- Add a replay harness that can re-play recorded server events (for unit tests and debugging). The harness must support time-dilation and injection of network anomalies (gaps, duplications).
- Ship a developer guide with recipes and three runnable examples under examples/streaming-middleware: 1) telemetry-only sideband sink, 2) deterministic replayer test, 3) graceful backpressure-aware retry wrapper example.

Non-goals: full rewrite of SDK streaming internals, replacing consumer-facing event schema (v1 contract only). We will not implement a distributed checkpointing system in this ticket.
acceptance_criteria: Small stable middleware API exported from redwood.sdk.streaming.middleware that accepts both sync generator and async-iterator consumers
Three middleware primitives implemented: signal_sanitizer, idempotent_sink_wrapper, retry_bridge with documented behavior and unit tests
Replay harness that can replay a JSONL trace into the middleware pipeline and a test that asserts deterministic replay behavior
Developer guide (docs/streaming_middleware.md) with at least three recipe examples and one end-to-end example app in examples/streaming-middleware
Benchmark: middleware adds <2% median latency overhead and <5% p99 overhead under our local microbench harness (results uploaded to perf dashboard)
API reviewed and approved by SDK lead and one runtime engineer (PR + review comments resolved)
Automated tests added to CI and examples runnable with `python -m examples.streaming_middleware.run_all`

snippets_examples:
# Minimal async middleware registration example:
from redwood.sdk.streaming import register_middleware, StreamingClient

async def signal_sanitizer(event, nxt):
    if event.get('tag') == 'telemetry':
        return  # drop
    return await nxt(event)

register_middleware(signal_sanitizer)
client = StreamingClient()
# client.chat_stream(...) now runs through middleware pipeline

# Sync shim for generator-style consumers:
def shim_sync_middleware(sync_consumer):
    async def wrapper(event, nxt):
        # convert event to sync-compatible call then call sync_consumer
        sync_consumer(event)
        return await nxt(event)
    return wrapper

# Replay harness usage:
$ python -m examples.streaming_middleware.replay --trace traces/large_convo.jsonl --time-dilation 10 --inject-gap 0.02
notes_and_tradeoffs: Chosen async-only middleware contract reduces maintenance surface (single code path) but requires a small shim for sync generator users — acceptable because most heavy consumers already use async flows.

Signal categorization (core/meta/telemetry) introduces a small coupling to event tagging but makes sanitization deterministic and easy to reason about for apps that must never surface telemetry to end-users.
Retry_bridge is intentionally conservative: it retries only idempotent 'partial' deltas and never retries events marked 'done' to avoid duplication at the transcript level.
Replay harness intentionally does not simulate all real-world TCP behaviors (out-of-order) in V1 — we add those if customer demand appears or for a follow-up test-only tool.
Performance: middleware is designed to run small, inline async call chains. If we see >5% overhead in customer workloads we will add an opt-in C-extension fast-path for critical hot loops.
